body:
This worries me more than the above: if we start introducing the partial-sum here, there's a large likelihood that commentators can disrail us to only leave this option.  This feels like a case of "anticipatory obedience".

Given that both p=1 and p=0 are valid — and implementations don't have to implement both — we gain nothing from having these specified.  This is a declaratory mechanisms at best and should be handled out-of-band.  If we avoid (over)specifying here, then implementors can define a "psm"-extension that they comply to ... it will declare the behaviour, but not prescribe it.  This way, applications that rely on psm=1, can pick hardware implementations that declare and conform to this extension.

My recommendation: drop the partial sums from the normative text; add an informative note that directs everyone towards the "declaratory extension" path if they want to differentiate themselves through psm.  We then add an ELF-flag that describes "I need PSM" and the kernel refuses to execute binaries if the ACPI tables don't declare PSM.  Everybody will be happy.

I don't think I fully understand. The `psm` parameter is not explicit in the architecture. It does not show in any CSR or something like that. It is an implementation choice. But we need to know what the choice is so that the SAIL behavior can be properly defined. Otherwise, how to write the formal specification?

My intent was to include G, psm, and the rounding mode in the geometry configuration in SAIL. Then, the code that define the instruction can use them. And I am letting the implementor specify their value in the processor datasheet, which I thought is what you had suggested at our previous meeting.

Would it help if I modified the SAIL code accordingly? I was planning on doing that this weekend anyway. We can then review on Monday during our (small) meeting.

Otherwise, please explain the issue in more detail for me.
